doctrine:
**A superior public officer cannot be held civilly liable for a subordinate's unremitted collections without a clear showing of bad faith, malice or gross negligence.** Under Section 38, Chapter 9, Book I of the Administrative Code of 1987, a public officer is not civilly liable for acts done in the performance of official duties unless there is a clear showing of bad faith, malice or gross negligence. A superior officer is not civilly liable for the wrongful acts, omissions, negligence or misfeasance of subordinates unless he actually authorized by written order the specific act or misconduct complained of. Under Sections 16.1 and 16.2 of the 2009 Rules and Regulations on the Settlement of Accounts (RRSA), liability for audit charges is measured by each officer's duties and individual participation in the charged transaction.

**Gross negligence** is the want of even slight care: acting or failing to act where there is a duty to act, "not inadvertently but willfully and intentionally with a conscious indifference to consequences." For public officials, it is a breach of duty that is flagrant and palpable. It must be proved by evidence and **cannot be inferred from speculation** that a subordinate's failure to remit resulted from the superior's failure to monitor or remind him. A COA finding of ordinary negligence (failure to observe the diligence of a good father of a family) is not enough.

Payment of the charge by the principal obligor extinguishes the solidary obligation (Civil Code, Art. 1217), but the case is not moot while other issues remain, such as the finding of liability itself and the referral to the Ombudsman. The Court may relax the rules on finality in its equity jurisdiction when the merits and special circumstances warrant (applied).
facts:
On September 17, 2010, Arnel Tabije was designated Special Collection Officer (SCO) at the Collection Division, Customs District II-A, Bureau of Customs (BOC). He stopped reporting for work in December 2010. Petitioner Rafael Crisol, Jr., Chief of the Cash Division, reported Tabije's irregular attendance and AWOL on December 9, 2010. In January 2011 he conducted a preliminary audit, which showed that Tabije had failed to deposit his collections and to turn over the auction fund passbook. On February 28, 2011 he directed Tabije in writing to settle the shortage. The matter was referred to the COA, and Tabije was administratively charged with dishonesty, unauthorized absences, inefficiency and gross neglect of duty.

The COA auditors issued Notice of Charge No. 2011-001-101(10), dated October 12, 2011, for Php425,555.53. It named as liable Tabije, District Collector Atty. Rogel Gatchalian (head of office) and Crisol. The COA NGS Cluster A Director (Decision No. 2012-006, June 8, 2012) excluded Gatchalian and Crisol, finding that they had been included merely because of their positions. On automatic review, the COA (Decision No. 2016-331, November 9, 2016) upheld Gatchalian's exclusion for lack of bad faith, malice or gross negligence, but reinstated Crisol's liability. It reasoned that as Chief with direct supervision over a new SCO, Crisol should have monitored Tabije's transactions, which were not deposited on time and not reported for September to November 2010. He was thus negligent, "jointly and solidarily liable," and, since Tabije had absconded, directly liable for the full amount. The COA also referred the case to the Ombudsman. Reconsideration was denied on September 7, 2017.

Crisol filed a Rule 64 petition. The COA later issued a Notice of Finality of Decision dated December 5, 2018 and told Crisol that only a direct order of the Supreme Court could stay finality. In a Manifestation dated February 14, 2019, Crisol reported that Tabije had fully paid the Php425,555.53, as shown by an official receipt and a Notice of Settlement dated February 7, 2019. He still asked the Court to rule on the merits.
issues: Whether the Court may resolve the petition despite the COA's issuance of a Notice of Finality of Decision.
Whether Tabije's full settlement of the charge rendered the petition moot.
Whether the COA gravely abused its discretion in holding Crisol solidarily liable for his subordinate's unremitted collections.
ruling:
**1. Yes; the Court relaxed the technical rules.** The Court acknowledged that final judgments are immutable, subject to recognized exceptions, and that perfecting an appeal within the period is jurisdictional. It also noted that it may relax procedural rules to serve substantial justice, considering among others: matters of property; special or compelling circumstances; the merits of the case; a cause not entirely attributable to the fault of the party favored; the lack of any showing that the review is frivolous; and the absence of unjust prejudice to the other party. The full settlement of the unremitted collection while the petition was pending, and, "more importantly, the merits of the case," justified relaxing the rules in the exercise of its equity jurisdiction.

**2. No, the case is not moot.** Under Section 13.1.2 of the 2009 RRSA, a charge is settled by payment or other modes of extinguishing obligations. Under Article 1217 of the Civil Code, payment by one of the solidary debtors extinguishes the obligation. Tabije's payment extinguished the civil liability, but the question remained whether Crisol could have been held solidarily liable "in the first place." The COA had also directed that the case be referred to the Ombudsman. Citing Peñafrancia Sugar Mill and Ilusorio, the Court held that the mootness of one issue does not warrant dismissal when other issues remain to be resolved.

**3. Yes, the COA gravely abused its discretion.** Section 38 of the Administrative Code requires a clear showing of bad faith, malice or gross negligence before a public officer becomes civilly liable, and a superior is not liable for a subordinate's wrongful acts unless he authorized them by written order. The COA applied this standard to exclude Gatchalian, yet made no finding of bad faith, malice or gross negligence against Crisol; it found him merely negligent. **"Gross negligence cannot be automatically inferred from mere speculation that a subordinate's failure to remit collections resulted from his superior's failure to monitor his transactions and remind him to comply with the relevant rules and regulations."** Every public officer is expected to comply with the rules, whether or not he is new to the post and whether or not a superior reminds him. Even if Crisol had a duty to remind, failing to do so is not gross negligence. His listed duties did not require him to monitor every deposit of each collection officer. Under Section 21 of the NGAS Manual, it was Tabije who had to deposit his collections intact daily or not later than the next banking day. There was no evidence of any badge of participation or conspiracy. Ideally, Crisol should have noticed Tabije's missing reports as early as September 2010. But his oversight was not gross negligence, given that he reported Tabije's AWOL, conducted the preliminary audit that uncovered the shortage, and demanded settlement. These acts "directly set in motion" the investigation, and without them the money might never have returned to the government.
disposition: The petition was GRANTED. The COA Decision dated November 9, 2016 and Resolution dated September 7, 2017 were REVERSED and SET ASIDE insofar as they held Crisol civilly liable under Notice of Charge No. 2011-001-101(10).

bar_questions.q: Mario, Chief of the Collection Division of a government agency, supervises 15 collecting officers. One of them, Jose, who was newly assigned, failed to deposit PHP 600,000.00 in collections for three months and then disappeared. When Jose stopped reporting, Mario reported his absences, audited Jose's accounts, discovered the shortage, and demanded that Jose pay. The COA issued a Notice of Charge holding Mario solidarily liable with Jose. It reasoned that the loss could have been avoided had Mario monitored Jose's daily deposits and reminded him of the deposit rules, so Mario failed to observe the diligence of a good father of a family. Is Mario civilly liable?

alac.answer: No. Mario is not civilly liable for Jose's unremitted collections.
alac.legal_basis: Under Section 38(1) and (3), Chapter 9, Book I of the Administrative Code of 1987, a public officer is not civilly liable for acts done in the performance of official duties unless there is a clear showing of bad faith, malice or gross negligence. A superior officer is not civilly liable for the wrongful acts or negligence of subordinates unless he actually authorized by written order the specific act or misconduct. In Crisol v. COA (G.R. No. 235764, September 14, 2021), the Court held that gross negligence must be proved and cannot be inferred from speculation that a subordinate's failure to remit resulted from the superior's failure to monitor and remind him.
alac.application: The COA found only ordinary negligence, a failure to observe the diligence of a good father of a family, and made no finding of bad faith, malice or gross negligence. The supposed lapse, failing to monitor and remind, is only speculatively linked to the loss, since every collecting officer must follow the deposit rules with or without reminders. Mario did not authorize Jose's failure to deposit by written order. His prompt report, audit and demand show he did not act with conscious indifference to the consequences.
alac.conclusion: Mario cannot be held civilly liable, and the COA's charge against him is grave abuse of discretion.

bar_questions.q: Same facts as in the previous problem, except that Mario, to "save on bank trips," issued a written memorandum authorizing Jose to keep his collections in the office vault and deposit them only once a month, contrary to the rule requiring daily deposit. Jose absconded with three weeks of collections. Is Mario civilly liable?

alac.answer: Yes. Mario may be held civilly liable because he authorized by written order the specific act that caused the loss.
alac.legal_basis: Section 38(3), Chapter 9, Book I of the Administrative Code of 1987 exempts a superior officer from civil liability for a subordinate's wrongful acts or omissions unless he actually authorized by written order the specific act or misconduct complained of. Section 38(1) also makes a public officer liable upon a clear showing of bad faith, malice or gross negligence. Under the 2009 RRSA, as applied in Crisol v. COA (G.R. No. 235764, September 14, 2021), liability for audit charges is measured by each officer's duties and individual participation in the charged transaction.
alac.application: In Crisol, the superior had no part in the subordinate's failure to remit. Here, Mario's written memorandum directly authorized the monthly, rather than daily, deposits that let Jose accumulate the collections and abscond with them. That falls squarely within the exception in Section 38(3). By deliberately authorizing a practice contrary to the deposit rules, Mario also participated in the charged transaction.
alac.conclusion: Mario may be held civilly liable for the loss.

bar_questions.q: Ana filed a Rule 64 petition questioning a COA decision that held her solidarily liable with her subordinate for a PHP 300,000.00 charge. The COA decision also referred the matter to the Ombudsman for possible charges against both of them. While the petition was pending, the subordinate paid the full amount, and the COA moved to dismiss Ana's petition as moot. (a) What is the effect of the subordinate's payment on the obligation? (b) Should the petition be dismissed as moot?

alac.answer: (a) The payment extinguished the obligation. (b) No, the petition is not moot.
alac.legal_basis: A charge is settled by payment or other modes of extinguishing obligations (2009 RRSA, Sec. 13.1.2), and payment made by one of the solidary debtors extinguishes the obligation (Civil Code, Art. 1217). A case is moot only when it no longer presents a justiciable controversy, so that a ruling would have no practical value; the mootness of one issue does not warrant dismissal if other issues remain. In Crisol v. COA (G.R. No. 235764, September 14, 2021), the Court ruled on whether the superior could have been held solidarily liable "in the first place," even though the principal had paid in full, because the COA had also referred the case to the Ombudsman.
alac.application: (a) The subordinate's full payment extinguished the civil obligation to the government. (b) Ana, however, still has a live interest in whether she was properly found solidarily liable, and the COA's referral to the Ombudsman, which rests on that finding, remains. A ruling on the merits therefore has practical value.
alac.conclusion: The obligation is extinguished, but the Court should resolve Ana's petition on the merits instead of dismissing it as moot.

notes: The decision begins its procedural discussion with the general rule against entertaining Rule 64 petitions that question the COA's dismissal of late appeals, but the facts it narrates do not show a late appeal; the relaxation appears tied to the Notice of Finality issued while the petition was pending. The decision calls petitioner's office both the "Cash Division" and the "Cash Collection Division," and gives the shortage as Php425,555.52 at one point and Php425,555.53 elsewhere. The Court did not rule separately on the referral to the Ombudsman; the fallo reverses the COA only insofar as it held Crisol civilly liable.
